findings.target: cmd/api/main.go:349 (WriteTimeout: 15s) + internal/httpx (no compression anywhere) + GET /v1/logbook's unbounded body
findings.finding: GET /v1/logbook answers 200 with a valid ETag header and a SILENTLY TRUNCATED body when the body divided by the link speed exceeds 15 seconds. There is no Content-Encoding, no Accept-Encoding handling, no Vary, and no ceiling on the read — so the only bound on the response is http.Server.WriteTimeout, which cuts the chunked stream mid-token and reports nothing. The plan's 1 MiB ceiling is on the WRITE; the read has none, and this is what that asymmetry costs.
findings.evidence: Executed against a real server (own build, own port 8477, own Postgres on 5477) holding a plausible ten-year log (350 trips, 600 cities, 850 places, 14,200 photographs, 100 walks of 1,200 points), emitted body 11,102,597 bytes. `curl --limit-rate 400k` -> HTTP/1.1 200 OK, `Etag: W/"1-35"`, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, 8,371,312 bytes received, curl exit 18, `json.load` -> `Unterminated string starting at char 8371258`; the last bytes on disk are `{"lat":35.0409862745072,"lng`. At 500 kB/s: 9,631,256 of 11,102,597 bytes, code 200. At 200 kB/s: 5,622,648 bytes, code 200. Unthrottled the same request is 151.9 ms and complete. No grep hit for gzip/Content-Encoding/Accept-Encoding anywhere outside tests.
findings.fix: Two independent halves, and the first is three lines. (1) Compress: measured on THE REAL client fixture, `gzip -6` takes 85,422 -> 5,479 bytes (15.6x); through the emitter at fixture scale, gzip level 1 takes 99,271 -> 6,806 bytes (14.6x) in 0.3 ms, and level 1 on the 11.1 MB log gives 2,084,727 bytes (5.3x) in 47.2 ms. That moves the 11 MB case from 'needs 740 kB/s sustained' to 'needs 139 kB/s'. (2) Raise WriteTimeout, or make it a function of body size, or state the ceiling: at 15s the server is promising that no log will ever exceed 15 seconds of the client's downlink, and nothing enforces that. Compression alone does not remove the class, it moves the threshold by ~6-15x.

findings.target: internal/auth/service.go:290 + internal/postgres/auth_store.go:175 (TouchSession under WithTravellerLock), on EVERY authenticated request
findings.finding: Every authenticated request — including a 304 that reads nothing — runs a full write transaction that takes the traveller's advisory lock to stamp `last_used_at`. So a conditional GET is 9 database round trips, 5 of them for a timestamp, and it serialises against the phone's own in-flight writes through the same `pg_advisory_xact_lock`. tx.go's comment argues at length that sessions must NOT bump `logbook_version`, which is correct and is a different question from whether they should take the write lock.
findings.evidence: pg_stat_statements reset, then exactly one 304 request. Nine statements: `begin`, `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended($1::uuid::text,0))` 0.023 ms, `SELECT 1 FROM travellers` 0.011 ms, `UPDATE sessions SET last_used_at` 0.077 ms, `commit`, plus `SELECT s.id, s.traveller_id, s.token_hash…` 0.041 ms, then `begin isolation level repeatable read read only`, `SELECT logbook_version FROM travellers` 0.010 ms, `rollback`. Total server exec 0.176 ms; wall clock for the 304 is 3.0-4.0 ms end to end, so it is round trips and not work. Contention measured separately: 6 concurrent writes on ONE traveller 34.95 ms vs 17.50 ms spread over 6 travellers.
findings.fix: Either take TouchSession out of the traveller's advisory lock (it writes one row keyed by session id; the lock buys it nothing that the row lock does not), or make it granular — only write `last_used_at` when the stored value is more than N minutes old, which turns a per-request write into a per-hour one. The existence check that WithTravellerLock does for it is a whole extra row read per request as well; the UPDATE's own `WHERE traveller_id` already answers that question.

findings.target: DEC-30 / DEC-49 — logbook_version as the whole-log cache key
findings.finding: Measured write amplification. The write itself is flat and cheap; what it costs is everyone's cached copy. A caption edit is one bump and then a full re-read of everything, and the ratio grows without bound with the log.
findings.evidence: Through the shipped store, per scenario — write ms / forced re-read ms / body bytes / amplification: 1x fixture 5.39 / 4.28 / 99,271 / 1x. 10x 5.12 / 14.59 / 991,675 / 3x. 100x 4.96 / 74.94 / 10,029,655 / 15x. 10x with 1,800-point tracks 6.19 / 40.44 / 2,821,305 / 7x. 50x with 1,200-point tracks 5.38 / 152.59 / 11,102,597 / 28x. The write cost does NOT grow with the log (4.9-6.2 ms across a 40x range); only the invalidation does.
findings.fix: The trigger for per-resource ETags is a number, and it is now available: it is when the forced re-read stops fitting the WriteTimeout budget of finding 1, which is the same threshold. Below ~1 MB the whole-log invalidation is cheaper than any per-resource scheme and DEC-31 is right. State the trigger as 'the emitted body exceeds N bytes' rather than 'when it feels slow', and measure N against the link, not against the server: the server side of the 100x re-read is 74.9 ms and the wire side at 1 Mbps is 80 seconds.

findings.finding: Yes — a legitimate request can exceed the 1 MiB ceiling, and it is the walk, not the place. `Walk.points` is a real recorded GPS track and the ceiling lands at 21,600 points, which is a six-hour walk at 1 Hz or a three-hour walk at 2 Hz. The client's own C2 screen draws `Walk.points` as a real polyline, so this is the field's actual purpose rather than a synthetic case.
findings.evidence: json.Marshal of logbook.Walk through the shipped types: 100 points 5,226 B; 1,000 points 51,004 B; 3,600 points 183,277 B; 10,000 points 508,964 B; 21,600 points 1,099,390 B (1.05 MiB, OVER); 30,000 points 1,526,804 B (1.46 MiB, OVER). For contrast the other array-carrying write, PUT /v1/places/{id}, needs ~10,000 visits on one place to cross it (1,800,155 B) against the fixture's worst case of 28 — never at this size.
findings.fix: Decide the ceiling on Walk.points explicitly and enforce it in ValidateWalk with its own 422 naming the field, so a long walk is refused with a sentence rather than by http.MaxBytesReader with `ErrBodyTooLarge` and no field name. Or raise MaxBodyBytes for that one route. The status quo is that a user's longest walk is the one write that silently cannot be saved.

findings.target: walks.points as jsonb inside the whole-log document — internal/postgres/logbook_store.go readWalkPointsSQL
findings.finding: Walk tracks, not photographs, are the whole-log read's real growth term, and the fixture hides this completely: its two walks carry 7 points BETWEEN THEM. Every argument in the plan about log size is calibrated on a log with no real track in it. Points also compress far worse than the rest of the document, because they are arrays of distinct floats.
findings.evidence: Same photograph count, tracks added: 10x with the fixture's own 3-4 point walks reads in 12.54 ms / 991,675 B; 10x with 1,800-point walks reads in 37.09 ms / 2,821,305 B — the 36,000 points cost 24.5 ms and 1.83 MB. gzip ratio on the photograph-heavy body is 15.6-17.5x; on the track-heavy body it is 4.4-6.2x. Server-side the unnest is honest: `Incremental Sort -> Nested Loop -> Memoize -> Function Scan on jsonb_array_elements`, 22.5 ms for 36,000 rows. NOTE ON METHOD: my first pass gave every walk an IDENTICAL track and Postgres's Memoize node cached it (`Hits: 19 Misses: 1`), understating the cost; the numbers above are from distinct tracks per walk.
findings.fix: Answer the open question first (see questions_for_human): if a track can be 20,000 points, it does not belong in the whole-log document at all — it is a media object fetched per walk, the same shape the photographs already use. If it is capped at a few hundred, it is fine where it is. The plan cannot choose between per-resource ETags and a whole-log read without this number.

findings.target: docs/plan-v7.json review_lenses_required (performance row), and every 'the log is 85 KB' argument in the plan
findings.finding: The emitted body at fixture scale is 99,271 bytes, not 85,422. The 85,422 figure is the CLIENT's format-1 document, whose assets are 31-32 character bundle paths; DEC-46 replaced those with 64-hex object ids, and DEC-40 stamps `"version": 2`. Every size argument in the plan is ~16% optimistic, and the drift is structural rather than a one-off: it grows with the photograph count.
findings.evidence: Loaded the real `internal/logbook/testdata/client_sample_log.json` (7 trips, 12 cities, 17 places, 49 visits, 284 photographs, 2 walks) into the shipped schema with assets hashed to sha256 as the schema's `photos_asset_sha256_ck` requires, read it back through `postgres.LogbookStore.Read` and `logbook.Emit`, and marshalled: 99,271 bytes. Fixture assets are `assets/imagery/hero-mountain.png` and `assets/imagery/card-ireland.png`; a sha256 id is 64 characters, so +32 bytes x 284 photographs plus covers.
findings.fix: Restate the premise number as 'the fixture emits 99,271 bytes through this build' with the derivation, rather than carrying the client's file size. It is one number in one place and it is the number DEC-31 rests on.

findings.target: internal/postgres/logbook_store.go:1 doc comment ('the six queries one read is made of') and read_tx.go
findings.finding: One whole-log read is TEN SELECTs, not six. read_tx.go's 'six lists' is a fair description of the document; logbook_store.go's 'six queries' is a count and it is wrong. This matters because the round-trip count is the thing that sets the floor on both the 200 and the 304 path, and the file that documents it is the one a reader would trust.
findings.evidence: pg_stat_statements after one read at 100x, one call each: photos, visits, trip_cities, places, cities, trips, walk_points, walks, `SELECT logbook_version FROM travellers`, `SELECT name FROM travellers` — ten — plus `begin isolation level repeatable read read only` and `rollback`.
findings.fix: Correct the count in the comment. Ten is also the number that makes the 3 ms 304 legible: it is 9 round trips at ~0.3 ms of latency each, over 0.176 ms of actual server work.

findings.target: internal/postgres/logbook_store.go — requireCities and replaceTripCities, inside WithTravellerTx
findings.finding: PutTrip is TWO round trips per child inside the advisory lock: one `SELECT 1 FROM cities` per city id, then one INSERT per city after the DELETE. Perfectly linear and irrelevant for trips, whose worst case in the fixture is 5 cities. It is worth stating once because the same shape is what the plan's PUT /v1/places/{id} will have with its whole visits array, and the fixture already holds a place with 28 visits and a real ten-year log would hold more.
findings.evidence: Measured against 1,200 real city rows: 1 city 3.32 ms, 5 cities 5.02 ms, 20 cities 14.00 ms, 100 cities 66.07 ms, 400 cities 249.85 ms, 1,200 cities 780.77 ms. Slope 0.63 ms per child, all of it inside the traveller's write lock.
findings.fix: Nothing for trips. For PUT /v1/places/{id}, do the existence check as one `= ANY($2)` and the insert as one multi-row INSERT (the loader I wrote does exactly this and loads 28,400 photographs in 1.37 s). Note the wire-protocol cap the database lens already found: 65,535 bind parameters, so batch.

findings.target: cmd/api/main.go:289 serverChain — httpx.Timeout has zero production call sites
findings.finding: No handler has a deadline. `httpx.Base` (which includes Timeout) is called by nothing outside tests, `serverChain` is Base minus Timeout by decision, and there is no `statement_timeout` or `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` on the runtime DSN either. So a stalled query holds a pool connection and an open REPEATABLE READ snapshot until the query finishes; WriteTimeout closes the socket at 15 s but does not cancel the handler goroutine or the transaction. The DBA review and the database lens both raised the Postgres half; this adds that the middleware which would have bounded the Go half is written and unwired.
findings.evidence: grep across the tree: `httpx.Timeout` appears only in middleware.go's own definition and in comments; `statement_timeout`/`idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` appear only in CLAUDE.md and the two review documents, never in code, a DSN or an env file. serve() sets ReadHeaderTimeout 5s, WriteTimeout 15s, IdleTimeout 60s and nothing else.
findings.fix: Either wire Timeout(d) with a config value, or delete it and say plainly in CLAUDE.md that the only request bound is WriteTimeout — right now the code reads as though a timeout exists. Adding `options=-c statement_timeout=5s` to the DSN is the cheaper half and closes the transaction leak that the Go-side timeout would not.

findings.target: DEC-21 / internal/auth/hasher.go DefaultParams — untuned in the direction of TOO CHEAP
findings.finding: Giving DEC-21's untuned parameters a shape, as asked. 64 MiB / t=1 / p=4 costs 20 ms per verify on this machine — that is fast for a passphrase KDF, and the risk it leaves open is a weak work factor rather than a resource ceiling. The concurrency cap is doing its job and is not the binding constraint at ARGON2_MAX_CONCURRENT=2.
findings.evidence: Apple M2 (Mac14,15), 8 cores, 16 GB. hash 19.9 ms, verify(correct) 20.0 ms, verify(wrong) 18.5 ms. Concurrency, wall clock and peak Argon2 memory: x1 20.1 ms / 64 MiB; x2 28.5 ms / 128 MiB; x4 75.1 ms / 256 MiB; x8 139.4 ms / 512 MiB; x16 249.2 ms / 1024 MiB; x32 638.3 ms / 2048 MiB. Parameter sweep at p=4: m=16 MiB t=1 14.1 ms, m=64 MiB t=1 26.6 ms, m=64 MiB t=2 59.6 ms, m=128 MiB t=1 59.6 ms, m=128 MiB t=2 104.6 ms, m=128 MiB t=3 135.1 ms. The live stack runs ARGON2_MAX_CONCURRENT=2 and AUTH_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MIN=10, so the real ceiling is 128 MiB and ~28.5 ms worst-case latency — comfortable against DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS=8.
findings.fix: The parameters are PHC-encoded so raising them is free for existing hashes (hasher.go already makes this point). At the current cap of 2, m=128 MiB t=2 would cost 104.6 ms per verify and 256 MiB peak — still small, and roughly 5x the work factor. The number this needs is not a benchmark, it is a login rate; nothing in the project has one. One traveller means the honest answer is 'raise it until sign-in is annoying', which is a real answer at this size.
findings.matters_at: never at this size (as a capacity question); now (as a work-factor question)

findings.target: internal/postgres/logbook_store.go — the Go scan half of the read
findings.finding: Worth stating once so nobody optimises the SQL: at 100x, 39% of the read is Go, not Postgres. The queries are already fine; the row-to-struct scanning through database/sql is the other half.
findings.evidence: One 100x read. Server exec time summed from pg_stat_statements: photos 20.79 + visits 5.92 + trip_cities 4.01 + places 2.67 + cities 1.68 + trips 1.18 + walk_points 0.51 + walks 0.27 + version 0.02 + name 0.00 + begin 0.01 = 37.06 ms. The same read measured in Go around `store.Read`: 61.20 ms. Difference 24.1 ms.
findings.fix: None warranted. Stated so that a future pass does not spend effort on query plans that are already sane and leave the larger term untouched.

findings.finding: Answering the question as asked: the batching is already right in the plan (mint takes a LIST and answers a list, 'a twelve-photo grid is one round trip, not twelve'), and the presign itself is free. Measured rather than assumed, since the prompt asked for it.
findings.evidence: AWS SigV4 presign crypto in Go — four chained HMAC-SHA256s over the signing key plus a SHA-256 over the canonical request, over a realistic 64-hex object key: 2.0 microseconds each, 20,000 iterations. Twelve = 0.024 ms. 284 = 0.6 ms. 28,400 = 56 ms.
findings.fix: Nothing. Do not add a cache, a batch store method or a background minter for this; OE-1 and OE-2 already declined those and the number says they were right by three orders of magnitude.

verified_correct: DEC-31'S CONDITIONAL READ IS THE STRONGEST THING IN THIS DESIGN, AND IT MEASURES THAT WAY. End to end through the real server: the 304 path is 3.03 / 3.38 / 3.99 / 3.41 / 3.12 / 3.16 ms across scenarios spanning 99 KB to 11.1 MB — CONSTANT, because the version is read inside the snapshot before anything is assembled. In-process, without the auth touch, it is 0.87-0.94 ms and equally flat. The callback-rather-than-document shape of Store.Read is what buys that and it is worth defending.

AT THE ACTUAL SIZE THIS THING IS, IT IS FAST AND NOTHING NEEDS DOING. The real client fixture — 7 trips, 12 cities, 17 places, 49 visits, 284 photographs — is 6.9 ms for a full 200 end to end over HTTP (4.2 ms read + 0.003 ms emit + 0.25 ms encode), 99,271 bytes, 3.0 ms for a 304, and a write is 5.4 ms. On a phone over any usable link the whole log arrives in well under a second. Everything in the findings above is about growth, not about now.

NO N+1 ANYWHERE IN THE READ. Every child list is one bulk query for the whole traveller plus a map from parent id to children — trip_cities and visits both, exactly as logbook_store.go's comment claims. Confirmed by pg_stat_statements: ten statements, `calls = 1` on every one, regardless of 7 trips or 700.

THE ADVISORY LOCK IS NOT HELD LONGER THAN IT NEEDS TO BE. 6 concurrent writes on one traveller: 34.95 ms, i.e. 5.8 ms each cleanly serialised, against 5.38 ms for a single write. Spread over 6 travellers the same 6 writes take 17.50 ms. Linear, no convoy, no pathology. The phone having several writes in flight costs exactly the sum of their service times.

A HELD READ SNAPSHOT DOES NOT BLOCK A WRITE, and I checked this specifically because it is the obvious worry. A write to the SAME traveller whose 100x read is in flight: 9.17 ms. A write to a DIFFERENT traveller during the same read: 15.55 ms. The different-traveller case is SLOWER, which proves the slowdown is CPU on a shared laptop and not lock or snapshot interaction. `WithReadSnapshot` taking no advisory lock is correct and measurably free.

THE WRITE PATH DOES NOT GROW WITH THE LOG. PutTrip is 5.39 / 5.12 / 4.96 / 6.19 / 4.90 / 5.38 ms across a 40x span of log sizes. The bump, the lock and the upsert are all indexed single-row operations and they behave like it.

QUERY PLANS ARE SANE AND THE PLANNER IS RIGHT TO DECLINE INDEXES ON THE SMALL TABLES. At 100x: photos is `Index Scan using photos_pkey` (10.777 ms, 28,400 rows); trips/trip_cities/places/visits are Seq Scan + quicksort, which is correct when 82% of a 5-page table matches. walks_pkey is used for both walk queries. Nothing is scanning what it should not.

THE RATE LIMITER'S MAP IS BOUNDED. `limiterPruneAbove = 1024` with a sweep of idle buckets, and it is a var so the pruning leg can lower it. Unbounded map growth was the failure this class of code usually has and this one does not have it.

NO BLOAT ON THE HOT ROWS, and I looked because the prompt asked. travellers: 294 updates, 294 HOT (100%), 42 dead tuples, 48 kB. sessions: 489 updates, 489 HOT (100%), 3 dead tuples, 64 kB. `logbook_version` and `last_used_at` are both unindexed, so every update is HOT and autovacuum keeps up trivially. 200 consecutive conditional GETs moved n_dead_tup from 31 to 59. This is a non-issue at one traveller and would stay one at a hundred.

THE POOL IS NOT THE CONSTRAINT. With DB_MAX_OPEN_CONNS=8, whole-log reads of the 10 MB log plateau at 24.2 reads/s (1 worker 13.3/s, 4 workers 19.7/s, 8 workers 23.5/s, 16 workers 24.2/s) — the plateau is the machine's CPU, not the pool, and 16 workers queueing on 8 connections costs nothing over 8. At the real fixture size the ceiling is far above anything one traveller can generate.

THE REPEATABLE-READ SNAPSHOT COSTS A HELD VIEW AND NOTHING ELSE, as read_tx.go claims. Longest snapshot measured: 152.66 ms. Nothing about a 150 ms xmin horizon threatens vacuum. (The DBA review's concern about an INDEFINITELY held snapshot is real and is the same gap as the missing statement_timeout in finding 9 — it is about a stall, not about the normal path.)

walks.points AS jsonb UNNESTED IN SQL RATHER THAN DECODED IN GO IS NOT COSTING ANYTHING AT THE FIXTURE'S SHAPE: 0.51 ms for 700 points across 200 walks at 100x. The encoding/json monopoly argument that put it there is not being paid for. It only becomes the dominant term when tracks are real (finding 5).
questions_for_human: WHAT IS THE REAL CEILING ON Walk.points, IN POINTS? This is the single number that decides three separate things and none of them can be settled without it: whether PUT /v1/walks/{id} fits the 1 MiB body ceiling (it stops fitting at 21,600 points), whether the whole-log read stays small enough for DEC-31 (100 walks of 1,200 points is 11.1 MB and 152 ms), and whether a track belongs in the log document at all or is a media object like a photograph. The fixture cannot answer it — its two walks carry 7 points between them — so every size argument in plan-v7 is calibrated on a log with no track in it.

IS COMPRESSION IN SCOPE FOR THIS PLAN, OR DOES IT BELONG TO THE CADDY SLICE? Finding 1 is a blocker as the stack stands, and a reverse proxy that terminates TLS and compresses would take most of it away. But Caddy is deferred to next_slice and DEF-01 is open, so today the Go server is the edge and there is nothing in front of it. Three lines of gzip middleware now, or a stated acceptance that the log must arrive in under 15 seconds until Caddy lands?

DOES `last_used_at` NEED PER-REQUEST GRANULARITY? It costs 5 of the 9 round trips on every authenticated request and it takes the traveller's write lock (finding 2). If it exists to show a human 'last seen about an hour ago', writing it only when the stored value is stale by more than a few minutes gives the same answer for a fraction of the cost. If something depends on it being exact, say what.
unverifiable: THE ENTIRE MEDIA PATH. `internal/media/` does not exist, go.mod has no minio-go (it has pgx and x/crypto and nothing else), and grep for minio/presign/Presign across the tree returns nothing outside the planning documents. R2, R3 and R8 have no code, which is the same wall the security lens hit. What I could measure is what a SigV4 presign costs in principle (finding 12); what the shipped implementation does, whether PresignHeader signs the length PD-11 needs it to, and what MinIO's own latency adds are all unmeasurable today.

THE 'BYTE CACHE KEYED BY OBJECT ID' NAMED IN THE BRIEF DOES NOT EXIST IN THIS REPOSITORY OR IN plan-v7, and I think the premise is wrong rather than the code missing. There is no server-side byte cache to bound because THE API NEVER HANDLES IMAGE BYTES AT ALL: POST /v1/media/mint answers presigned URLs and the phone fetches the bucket directly, and OE-12 keeps the store interface at three methods with no Get. So the answer to 'what is its size bound' is 'there is nothing to bound, by design' — which is worth recording as a design property rather than an omission. If the question is about the Flutter client's own image cache, that is the other repository and outside this lens.

GET /l/{token}'S PUBLIC ENVELOPE AND ITS JOINS. R8, no code, and docs/PUBLIC-ENVELOPE.md is written in R5 rather than existing. The row-multiplication question about it cannot be asked of anything yet.

THE PHONE'S JSON DECODE, WHICH I SUSPECT IS THE LARGEST SINGLE TERM AT SCALE AND I CANNOT MEASURE. Go's encode is 0.25 ms at fixture scale and 29.1 ms at 11.1 MB. Dart's `jsonDecode` of an 11 MB document on a mid-range phone, plus building 14,200 Photo objects through the generated codecs, is plausibly seconds and is on the main isolate unless the client moves it. Nothing in this repository can measure it; it needs the Flutter side and a device. It is the half of DEC-31's 'the log is small' argument that neither lens can reach.

REAL NETWORK NUMBERS. Everything above is loopback on one Apple M2 (Mac14,15, 8 cores, 16 GB) with PostgreSQL 17 in Docker, both processes competing for the same CPU. Treat the server-side timings as a floor and the concurrency figures as pessimistic — the truncation measurement in finding 1 used `curl --limit-rate` to simulate a slow link, which throttles the reader rather than the network, so the mechanism is proven but a real lossy mobile link may behave differently in detail.
